occurrence.title: Publication of Buffett's 2022 Annual Shareholder Letter
occurrence.subject_relevance: Warren Buffett authored and published the annual shareholder letter, his 45th such letter.
descriptions: Buffett published his 45th annual shareholder letter alongside Berkshire Hathaway's 2022 annual report and fourth-quarter results. The letter was noted as the shortest in 44 years at 4,455 words. It addressed Berkshire's large cash and Treasury holdings, stock repurchases, the company's long-term strategy, and Buffett's reflections on his investment decisions.

occurrence.title: Berkshire Hathaway sale of BYD shares in December 2022
occurrence.subject_relevance: The sale was made by Berkshire Hathaway, which Buffett leads as CEO. The source attributes the sale to Buffett's company.
descriptions: Berkshire Hathaway sold 1.3295 million Hong Kong-listed BYD shares at an average price of HK$201.3432 per share, reducing its stake from 15.07% to 14.95%. This was the sixth disclosed stake reduction in less than three months.

Following the December 8 sale, Berkshire had sold more than 13 million BYD shares in total since August, unwinding more than a quarter of its holdings; the sales had cashed out more than HK$3 billion over less than three months. BYD's Hong Kong-listed shares closed about 1.5% lower on the Tuesday of the filing, and had lost about 23% of market value since the end of August.

BYD Executive Vice President Stella Li played down Berkshire's sales, saying it was "very natural" for Buffett to get some returns and that the offloading was not an indication the investor was abandoning BYD; she said Buffett "loves" the company and its management and would always be its biggest supporter.

occurrence.title: Berkshire Hathaway acquisition of Alleghany Corporation
occurrence.subject_relevance: Buffett, as Berkshire Hathaway's CEO, described the acquisition as originating from an email he received from Alleghany's new CEO and his long-term interest in Alleghany; he arranged a meeting that led to the transaction.
descriptions: Berkshire Hathaway acquired Alleghany Corporation in a deal of over $11 billion. Buffett recounted at the 2022 annual meeting that he received an email from a friend who had become Alleghany's CEO, replied that he would read the annual report over the weekend, and proposed meeting in New York on March 7. He noted he had followed Alleghany for sixty years and had no acquisition plan when he received the email; without the email, Berkshire might never have made the investment.

occurrence.title: Berkshire Hathaway purchase of Occidental Petroleum shares
occurrence.subject_relevance: Warren Buffett, as Berkshire Hathaway's CEO, publicly described and explained the company's Occidental Petroleum share purchase at the 2022 annual meeting.
descriptions: Berkshire Hathaway bought about 14% of Occidental Petroleum's shares within two weeks, at a time when only about 60% of the shares were freely tradable. Berkshire already held preferred stock in Occidental.

At the April 30, 2022 annual meeting, Buffett retrospectively said that buying 14% of a company within two weeks, when only about 60% of shares were freely tradable, was not a good investment, and contrasted it with Berkshire's usual approach of taking a long time to buy a 14% stake.

Buffett said an Occidental analyst presentation around February 28 contained some things that did not sound very reasonable, but that after about two weeks of tracking it still seemed Berkshire's money could be invested in the company; he added that Berkshire could have bought more shares but investment timing cannot be predicted.

occurrence.title: Buffett's personal decision to invest in Activision Blizzard
occurrence.subject_relevance: Buffett stated the investment was his personal decision.
descriptions: Buffett said he personally decided to invest in Activision Blizzard a few months before the 2022 annual meeting, and continued buying shares because the price was below Microsoft's offer.

activity_detail.value: Berkshire bought $51.8 billion of stocks and sold $10.3 billion in Q1; bought $41 billion between late February and mid-March. Buffett said the company would retain sufficient safe cash and had not repurchased shares since April.

Buffett said Berkshire spent about $2 billion from January 1 to February 18, then unexpectedly deployed about $40 billion over roughly three weeks; in Q1 it spent around $3 billion on equities before rapidly deploying the $40 billion.
Buffett said he and Munger agreed Berkshire would always hold more than $30 billion in cash and equivalents.
Buffett said the past two years were volatile and hard to fathom, with the stock market like a casino where everyone was gambling, especially pronounced in the past two years.

Buffett said Berkshire does not buy or sell based on market or economic conditions because it does not know the actual situation; it buys when it thinks the investment is cheap. He noted Berkshire also failed to seize opportunities during the 2008 financial crisis.

Buffett said Berkshire spent a large portion of its capital during the 2008 downturn, roughly $15-16 billion over three to four weeks, and that if they truly knew the timing they might have waited another six months.
Buffett said he completely missed the March 2020 stock market decline and wished the downturn had lasted longer to allow more investment, since cheaper prices would mean more buying.

Buffett said the Activision Blizzard stake was entirely his personal decision made months earlier, and he had been buying more shares since the deal was announced because the stock traded well below Microsoft's offer price; if the deal closed, buying at those levels would generate greater returns.

Buffett said the Activision stake was a personal decision made months earlier, and he had continued buying because the shares traded well below Microsoft's offer price, which would yield greater returns if the deal closed.
Buffett said bitcoin does not produce value; its price depends only on what the next buyer will pay. Cryptocurrency may seem magically attractive due to hype but has no productive capacity.

Buffett illustrated bitcoin's lack of productivity by contrasting it with owning 1% of all U.S. farms or apartments, which would produce rent and output, whereas bitcoin produces nothing and its value depends on the next buyer.

Buffett said Berkshire's culture is first a hard-working company and second one that always cares about shareholders; culture accounts for 99.9% of a company's operation. Berkshire aims to exist for the next hundred years, build a better and more stable relationship with shareholders, and will hand the company to people it trusts.

Buffett said the best way to combat high inflation is to invest in yourself: become exceptionally good at something, be useful to society, and your skills will not be eroded by inflation. He said developing yourself is not taxed and that is what he is doing at this time.

Buffett said his own path to investing was somewhat accidental, influenced by his father and access to books. He advised finding what you truly want to do and doing it for a lifetime, finding the kind of world you want to live in, and working for people you truly respect.
Berkshire's Q1 2023 operating profit slightly exceeded $8 billion. Buffett noted long-term capital gains are substantial but stock price volatility can be large over single quarters or years.

Buffett described significant volatility over the past six months, possibly the worst since WWII, driven by excess inventory rather than unemployment. Many managers were surprised by unsold inventory; sales are slowly recovering but may be slower than last year.

Buffett said investment income in Q1 2023 was much larger than the prior year, a long-built advantage. Insurance underwriting is not fully correlated with market activity but tied to natural disasters; he expects underwriting to do better than last year.
Buffett reported float of $165 billion, growing significantly since 1986 without requiring employee effort or interest, and noted it carries obligations.

Buffett called the situation very painful, noted FDIC limits around $250,000, and said the debt ceiling has not yet reached a severe outcome. He expressed reluctance to explain the situation on television.
Buffett said he aims for balanced investment plans and decisions, and does not recall any emotional decisions in Berkshire's history.
Buffett praised Tod, the Geico CEO selected by him and Ajit Jain, for his work on matching rate and risk, and noted they meet on weekends to discuss business.
Buffett said no AI function can replace Ajit Jain, and noted Bill Gates showed him the latest technology, which progressed faster than he imagined.
Buffett said Greg Abel will inherit some of his work, but he remains in position and Abel may need others to replace him.

Buffett said Berkshire's investments in five Japanese trading companies yield about 14% for acquisitions, pay dividends, and sometimes buy back stock. Berkshire can eliminate currency risk via yen financing at 0.5% cost. Berkshire recently increased holdings to 7.4% and then to 9.9% without the companies' knowledge.

Buffett said Berkshire had prior business dealings with the five Japanese trading companies, including in coal-fired and gas-fired power plants, and that Berkshire had promised its holdings would not exceed 9.9%. He introduced Greg Abel to the companies for long-term cooperation over the next 10 to 40 years.

Buffett said Berkshire bought some Occidental common stock in recent months and disposed of preferred stock, believing the position remains favorable. He called it a smart decision to sell some preferred and continue holding common.

Buffett said Berkshire's position in Occidental is very favorable and that the management is outstanding. He noted he bought his first such stock in 1942 and understands the math but would be at a loss at an oil well.

Buffett said Berkshire's stock is undervalued, so it is not yet time to distribute cash. Berkshire prefers to buy excellent businesses for $25B to $75B or even $100B, but the company must be good. Public companies are difficult due to competing bids; returns of only 1-2% are not worthwhile.

Buffett said Berkshire's stock is undervalued and it is not yet time to distribute cash; Berkshire prefers buying excellent businesses for $25B to $75B or even $100B, but the company must be good. Public-company bids face competition, and returns of only 1-2% are not worthwhile. He noted some seemingly well-positioned companies resisted acquisition, citing Tiffany and Harley Davidson in 2008, and that some good companies only want $5B-$10B of capital rather than being sold entirely.
Buffett said he and Munger find the auto industry very tough. He recounted Henry Ford's early dominance and later losses, and said he has a different view, especially regarding the U.S.

The letter stated that Berkshire will always hold a large amount of cash and U.S. Treasury bills, as well as a wide range of businesses, and will avoid actions that could cause cash flow inconvenience during financial panics or unprecedented insurance losses.

Buffett wrote that Berkshire's purpose in holding equity is to make meaningful investments in businesses with long-term good economic characteristics and trustworthy managers, and that he and Charlie Munger choose companies, not stocks.
Buffett acknowledged making many mistakes over the years, noting that some businesses he invested in failed and that capitalism has a 'creative destruction' aspect.

Buffett defended stock repurchases, stating that anyone who says all buybacks are bad for shareholders or the country, or especially beneficial to CEOs, is either economically illiterate or a silver-tongued demagogue.

Buffett defended Berkshire's federal tax payments, stating the company paid $32 billion in federal taxes over the past decade, representing one-thousandth of all taxes collected by the government during that period.
Buffett criticized federal government spending far exceeding tax revenue and commented on the debt ceiling debate in Washington, stating that 'huge and entrenched fiscal deficits have consequences.'
Buffett stated that Berkshire would not be broken up, writing 'In Berkshire, there is no finish line,' and that the next CEO must hold a large portion of their net worth in Berkshire stock.
Buffett wrote that his capital allocation decisions were mostly 'so-so' and that Berkshire's satisfactory long-term results came from only about a dozen 'truly good' decisions.
Buffett wrote that trust and rules are essential for running a large enterprise even amid inevitable disappointments, and urged investors not to be fixated on recent market conditions.

Buffett wrote that Berkshire's CEO will always be the chief risk officer, and that the company will avoid reckless behavior that could cause cash-flow inconvenience at critical moments, including financial panics and unprecedented insurance losses.
Buffett noted that Berkshire spent $7.9 billion on stock repurchases in 2022, and the letter devoted much of its content to defending the company's practices including buybacks.
Buffett wrote that if about 1,000 taxpayers matched Berkshire's payments, no other business or any of the country's 131 million households would need to pay any federal tax — 'not a dime.'
Buffett stated that the decision to invest in Activision Blizzard shares was entirely his personal decision made a few months earlier.

Buffett said he had been buying more Activision shares since the deal was announced because the stock was trading well below Microsoft's offer price; he noted that if the deal closed, buying at those levels would generate a larger return.

巴菲特称，周五收市一分钟后致电霍鲁布，告知购股情况。这次联系发生在买入之后。
巴菲特把约两周取得约 14% 股份归因于市场频繁换手、可成交股票充足；这是他对前期执行过程的回述。
7 月 11 日申请许可；8 月 4 日表决权超过 20%；8 月 19 日获准买至 50%；年末持股 21.4%。许可上限不等于控股意图。
霍鲁布在 3 月 6 日采访中说，几天前与巴菲特见面，讨论油气行业及相关技术。
认可霍鲁布对石油和政治现实的理解，提到她关注碳捕集；预期未来五年仍需大量石油。
认可二叠纪资产，但油价未知；懂财务计算，不懂经营油田，愿由霍鲁布管理。不提出控股要约，保留增持可能。
滚动 12 个月普通股股东回报达到合同门槛，触发优先股强制赎回。5 月 9 日业绩报告披露已触发 6.47 亿美元赎回。
巴菲特不乐见优先股被赎回，同时认为这对西方石油是合理做法。这同时保留了他的投资偏好与对公司资本安排的评价。
霍鲁布称与巴菲特保持交流，谈话不限于商业；CrownRock 收购不需要伯克希尔提供融资帮助。
伯克希尔普通股持仓达到 243,715,804 股。当月逐笔买入的个人理由：材料未提供。
